clue.text: Trim some timber

definitions.meaning: trim as an adjective means neat and smart in appearance
the wood of a kind of fir tree

explanation.definitionFit: Spruce means neatly turned out, and it is also a conifer whose softwood is sold as timber.

clue.text: Like part of Russia's southern peninsula, for example

parts.note: Iberian describes the Spanish and Portuguese peninsula, one example of a peninsula

explanation.surface: A geography question likens part of Russia to a southern European peninsula.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Russia's southern peninsula' suggests Crimea, but the 's is only a link and 'southern' gives S.
explanation.definitionFit: Siberia is the vast Asian region of Russia, so anything from there is Siberian.

clue.text: Perfect example of a Prime Minister being cut short in the centre of Jarrow

indicators.note: in places the shortened statesman between the central letters
the centre of a six-letter town is its third and fourth letters
cut short says the name loses its last letter

parts.note: Clement Attlee was British Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister, a model of his kind, is trimmed down in the Tyneside town of Jarrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' drops the last letter of the statesman's name, and 'in' sets it between the middle letters of Jarrow, a town in north-east England famous for its 1936 hunger march.
explanation.definitionFit: Rattler is old slang for something excellent, a first-rate specimen of its kind.

clue.text: Instrument for the palmist

parts.note: not a fortune-teller's tool but a percussion instrument clicked while held in the palm of the hand

explanation.definitionFit: Castanets are pairs of shell-shaped wooden clappers held in the palm and clicked by the fingers.

clue.text: Old instrument case key returned in Lincoln

indicators.note: the word in tells us one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: Abe is the familiar name of President Abraham Lincoln

indicators.note: returned asks for the synonym of key to be read backwards

parts.note: key as an adjective means crucial, vital

explanation.surface: A museum piece: an antique musical instrument's carrying case, its key sent back to someone in the city of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' reverses the synonym of key, and 'in' places it within the President's nickname. 'Instrument' is not music: the Latin ablative case carries the old instrumental sense, 'by means of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin grammar's ablative case took over the work of the older instrumental case, expressing the means by which something is done.

clue.text: It produces a report, but not written on this kind of paper

parts.note: a blank sheet has nothing written on it
cartridge paper is a thick, strong drawing paper

explanation.surface: A news report is produced on blank paper, not written out by hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'report' looks like a written account, but it is the bang of a gun: a blank cartridge fires noise without a bullet.
explanation.definitionFit: A blank cartridge contains powder but no bullet, so firing it gives only the loud bang of a shot.

clue.text: Stroll round the island about a mile

indicators.note: about says the turned island goes around the mile
round turns the island's name the other way about

parts.note: Elba is the Mediterranean island of Napoleon's first exile
M abbreviates mile

explanation.surface: Someone takes a leisurely walk of about a mile around the island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' turns ELBA into ABLE, and 'about' wraps it around M.
explanation.definitionFit: To amble is to walk at a slow, relaxed pace, the same as a stroll.

clue.text: Eccentric fined £1 as an enemy of the faith

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or irregular, so the letters go out of their order

parts.note: L is the pound sign's letter, from Latin libra, and I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An oddball fined a pound is condemned as a heretic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' looks like a noun, a crank, but it rearranges FINED with L and I.
explanation.definitionFit: An infidel is an unbeliever, one who rejects or opposes a given religion.

clue.text: In the past it could be 'ringed'

definitions.text: In the past it could be 'ringed'

indicators.note: could be invites the letters of ringed to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned word turns out to mean a thing that has been encircled.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of RINGED gives a word for encircle that was used in former times, which is why the clue says 'In the past'.
explanation.definitionFit: Engird is an archaic verb meaning to surround or encircle, so something engirded was ringed.

clue.text: This mad king of ancient Greece had to join in marriage in a melodramatic way

indicators.note: mad tells us the letters of the word this run wild

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for king, from Latin rex
Ionic describes Ionia, part of ancient Greece, and its style of architecture
to ally is to unite, as by marriage

explanation.surface: An insane monarch of classical Greece is forced into a wedding with theatrical fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mad' rearranges the first word's letters; 'king of ancient Greece' looks like one person but splits into two pieces, the royal abbreviation and the architectural adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Histrionically means in a theatrical, overacted manner, which is what melodramatic behaviour is.

clue.text: Little woman mentioned a Galilean town

parts.note: Beth March is one of the sisters in Louisa May Alcott's novel Little Women
to have mentioned something is to have said it

explanation.surface: A small lady is reported to have named a town in Galilee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little woman' reads as a petite lady, but it points to one of the four March sisters in Alcott's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Bethsaida was a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee, named in the Gospels as home to several apostles.

clue.text: Obscure petition outside the Foreign Office

indicators.note: outside says the request word wraps around the abbreviation

parts.note: to petition is to beg
FO is the standard abbreviation for the British Foreign Office

explanation.surface: Someone presents an unclear petition on the pavement in front of the Foreign Office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' is a verb here, to make unclear, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To befog is to cloud or confuse, just as to obscure is to hide from clear view.

clue.text: Confident no initial inertial guidance is needed

indicators.note: guidance steers the remaining letters into a new order
no initial says the word inertial loses its opening letter

explanation.surface: A rocket engineer is sure the missile needs no inertial guidance system at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no initial' strips the I from INERTIAL to leave NERTIAL, and 'guidance' rearranges those seven letters. 'Inertial guidance' looks like one technical phrase but is split across two jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Being reliant on something means trusting and depending on it, which suggests confidence in it.

clue.text: He is said to want to become a masseur

indicators.note: is said tells us the word is heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: to want is to need, and the clue's He is the one who does so, a needer

explanation.surface: A man reportedly longs to train as a massage therapist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He ... to want' makes a man who needs, a NEEDER, and 'is said' turns that into a word with the same sound but a silent K, one who works muscles with the hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A masseur works the muscles by pressing and rolling them, as a baker works dough, so he is one who kneads.

clue.text: Suit needed for the Sea-green Incorruptible

indicators.note: needed for says the letters required sit within the following phrase

explanation.surface: Robespierre, nicknamed the Sea-green Incorruptible, has to be dressed in a fitting outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Carlyle called Robespierre 'the sea-green Incorruptible'; the answer runs across the hyphen of 'Sea-green'. 'Suit' is the verb, to be acceptable to.
explanation.definitionFit: If an arrangement suits you, it agrees with you: both mean to be acceptable or fitting.

clue.text: Claudio's sister was yellow

definitions.meaning: in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure the novice nun who pleads for her brother Claudio's life
a greyish-yellow or buff colour, especially of horses

explanation.definitionFit: Isabella is the heroine of Measure for Measure, sister of the condemned Claudio, and isabella is also a pale fawn-yellow shade.

clue.text: Putting out mere information on the church for Advent

indicators.note: putting out the word mere disturbs its letters

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A vicar puts out a little information about the church calendar for Advent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting out' rearranges MERE to EMER. GEN is British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: An advent is an arrival or coming into view, which is an emergence.

clue.text: Spout from the gutter

parts.note: not crude talk from a low-life but a carved stone waterspout projecting from a roof gutter

explanation.definitionFit: A gargoyle is a grotesque carved figure on a building that throws rainwater clear of the walls.

clue.text: Money, after tax, may do for a whole school

definitions.text: may do for a whole school

parts.note: a purse is a sum of money, as a prize purse
net pay is what remains after tax is deducted

explanation.surface: A head teacher wonders whether the post-tax budget will stretch to cover the whole school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' looks like pupils, but it is a school of fish: a net drawn closed like a purse can catch a whole shoal.
explanation.definitionFit: A purse-net is a bag net whose mouth is drawn shut with a cord, so it can enclose an entire shoal of fish.

clue.text: A. French Service, for example, being rude

parts.note: un is the French word for a
the Civil Service is one example of a service

explanation.surface: A French civil servant behaves impolitely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A. French' means the word 'a' in French; the Civil Service gives CIVIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncivil means lacking courtesy, which is to be rude.

clue.text: Schoolboy seen with a girl

parts.note: Eric is the schoolboy hero of the Victorian moral tale Eric, or Little by Little

explanation.surface: A schoolboy has been spotted out with a girlfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric, or Little by Little (1858) made Eric the archetypal earnest schoolboy, a stock crossword reference.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is a girl's given name, so it fits as an example of a girl.

clue.text: One object in China to copy

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: in puts the object word inside the friend word

parts.note: china is cockney rhyming slang for mate, from china plate
it is an object pronoun

explanation.surface: A single object made in China is a copy of something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is not the country: in cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means a friend, and 'in' puts the object pronoun inside that word.
explanation.definitionFit: To imitate is to mimic or reproduce, which is to copy.

clue.text: Sailors with the sun to soak up

parts.note: AB is an able seaman, so ABS are sailors
the sun is a heavenly orb

explanation.surface: Sailors lie out on deck to soak up the sunshine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the sun' is the shining orb in the sky, a poetic name for it.
explanation.definitionFit: To absorb is to take in liquid, which is what soaking up means.

clue.text: Getting a taxi back — smart of a reveller!

indicators.note: back asks for the taxi word to be read from right to left

parts.note: a cab is a taxi
chic means stylish or smart

explanation.surface: A partygoer, dressed sharply, hails a cab to get home after a night out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the taxi word; 'smart' is stylish, not clever, and 'of a reveller' is an adjectival definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacchic means relating to Bacchus, god of wine, and hence to drunken revelry.

clue.text: Stockings may be banned in hot weather

definitions.meaning: an old plural of hose, leg coverings

definitions.text: may be banned in hot weather
definitions.meaning: garden water pipes forbidden in drought

explanation.definitionFit: Hose is old legwear such as stockings, and hosepipes are prohibited when summer drought brings a hosepipe ban.

clue.text: Entry for one noggin — new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: new order means the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bar tab lists a single noggin of spirits, and a fresh round is ordered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new order' rearranges the six letters of NOGGIN, placed after I for one. 'Entry' is the act of going in, not an item in a list.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingoing is an entrance or entering, the act of going in.

clue.text: Stupid louts round S Stalky's pleasant isle

parts.note: a round shape is the letter O
in Kipling's Stalky & Co. Beetle names the boys' cliff-top hideout 'the pleasant isle of Aves'

explanation.surface: Dim hooligans surround the boys' secret retreat from Kipling's school stories.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's schoolboys call their hiding place 'the pleasant isle of Aves'; the lone S in the clue echoes the final letter and does no further work.
explanation.definitionFit: Oaves is an old plural of oaf, a clumsy, stupid person.

clue.text: Inscription has a line that is famous

parts.note: a legend is the inscription on a coin or medal
RY abbreviates railway, a line

explanation.surface: A monument's carved wording includes one celebrated line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' is a railway line here, abbreviated RY, not a line of text.
explanation.definitionFit: Something legendary is celebrated and widely known, as legends are.

clue.text: Boiled sweet a magpie won't touch

definitions.meaning: a hard, round, striped peppermint candy
in target shooting a magpie is a shot in the second ring from the outside, so it never hits the centre

explanation.definitionFit: A bull's-eye is a striped hard candy, and also the centre of a target, which a magpie, a shot in an outer ring, misses.

clue.text: Remove obstruction in river

indicators.note: in places the obstruction word inside the river

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and another between England and Wales
a let is a hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: Engineers clear a blockage from a river.
explanation.walkthrough: LET in the old sense of hindrance survives in tennis and in the passport phrase 'without let or hindrance'.
explanation.definitionFit: To delete is to strike out or erase, which is to remove.
